scenes.title: Choosing is a learning decision
scenes.visual: Founder reviews three anonymous problem cards.
scenes.narration: You have noticed problems, explored the people affected, considered possible causes, and looked at alternatives. Now choose one problem to explore further. This is a provisional learning decision. It does not prove demand, and you can change your focus when better evidence arrives.

scenes.title: Compare specific candidates
scenes.visual: Three editable cards share the same comparison headings.
scenes.narration: Describe each candidate as a person, a task and a situation. Compare why the difficulty may matter, what evidence you have, how you can reach people ethically, and whether a small next check is feasible. Keep unknowns visible. Do not choose only because an app would be exciting to build.

scenes.title: Evidence before enthusiasm
scenes.visual: Observer distinguishes planned notes from observed information.
scenes.narration: A vivid story is not the same as repeated evidence. Separate observations, reports, interpretations and planned research. Consider what existing approaches do well. If every candidate is still a hypothesis, say so. You can choose the most useful learning opportunity without inventing certainty.

scenes.title: Choose with reasons and tradeoffs
scenes.visual: Founder writes a provisional focus and a reconsideration trigger.
scenes.narration: Choose one candidate and explain your reasons. Record the strongest reason against it and why other candidates are parked. Avoid automatic scores that turn guesses into precision. If none is ready, narrow a candidate and plan a preliminary check. Record what would make you change your choice.

scenes.title: Make the next check practical
scenes.visual: Calendar and anonymous consent-based research plan.
scenes.narration: Choose one small next step: observe a permitted process or ask an adult about a recent experience. Name the setting, timing, permission needed and the question you want to answer. Set a signal that would support or weaken your focus. Do not collect private details you do not need or promise a solution.

scenes.title: Close the discovery module
scenes.visual: Actual worksheet recording and five-deliverable checklist.
scenes.narration: Create your Problem Selection Brief and review your journal, affected-people map, problem map and alternatives log. These five deliverables close Module 1.2 when each lesson is locally complete. This records learning, not a validated market. Next, develop a first customer snapshot with assumptions clearly labeled.

blocks.label: I read the transcript or reviewed the learning guide. Video is not required.

children: A
problem candidate
is a specific difficulty experienced by a particular person doing a task in a context. Your
provisional focus
is the candidate you will explore next, not a permanent commitment or a validated business.

Compare candidates using the same questions: How important might this be? What evidence supports it? Can you reach the people ethically? Can you investigate it with your available time and skills? What works well about their current approach?
Illustrative example:

an event founder compares finding registration, reconnecting after an event and locating session information. Each is only a candidate. Access to a permitted observation may make one easier to investigate; it does not prove it is the biggest market.
A fair selection process
Describe three candidates or clearly label a candidate still to find.
Use the same criteria; keep missing evidence unknown.
Choose a provisional focus and record a reason against it.
Park the others with a reason; do not discard their evidence.
Set a small next check and a trigger for reconsidering.
If none is sufficiently clear, choose a narrower research focus and explicitly record the uncertainty. You do not need to manufacture a winner.
Review your Module 1.2 work
Review discovery journal
Review affected people
Review problem map
Review alternatives log
